title: Meet Your Data: The Full Picture
instruction: Welcome, new recruit! Our database holds vital information. Your first mission: retrieve ALL data from the `employees` table to understand who's on our team. Show me everything!
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM employees
successMsg: Excellent! You've successfully viewed all employee data.
hint: To see every column and every row, use the wildcard character `*` after `SELECT`.

title: Focus on the Essentials: Employee Names and Departments
instruction: Great start! Now, the boss only needs a list of employee names and their respective departments. No need for their IDs or salaries this time. Can you select just the `name` and `department` columns from the `employees` table?
expectedQuery: SELECT name, department FROM employees
successMsg: Perfect! You've learned to select specific pieces of information.
hint: List the column names you want to see, separated by commas, after `SELECT`.

title: Find the 'Sales' Team
instruction: Our Sales department is planning a meeting. Can you find all employees who belong to the 'Sales' department? Retrieve all their details from the `employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = 'Sales'
successMsg: You've successfully filtered for specific departments! The Sales team appreciates it.
hint: Use the `WHERE` clause to filter rows based on a condition. Remember to put string values in single quotes.

title: High Earners: Employees Above $60000
instruction: Management wants to identify employees earning more than $60,000. Show me all details for employees whose `salary` is greater than 60000 from the `employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > 60000
successMsg: Great job! You can now filter data based on numeric comparisons.
hint: Comparison operators like `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` are your friends in the `WHERE` clause.

title: Find Employees with 'Manager' in Their Name
instruction: We need to find anyone whose name might indicate a managerial role, specifically names that contain 'Manager'. Use the `LIKE` operator and the wildcard `%` to find employees from the `employees` table whose `name` contains the substring 'Manager'.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE name LIKE '%Manager%'
successMsg: Excellent use of `LIKE`! Pattern matching is a powerful tool.
hint: `%` matches any sequence of zero or more characters. Use it with `LIKE`.

title: Double Conditions: IT & High Salary
instruction: We're looking for experienced IT professionals. Find all employees who work in the 'IT' department AND have a `salary` greater than or equal to $70,000. Show all their details from the `employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = 'IT' AND salary >= 70000
successMsg: You've mastered combining conditions with `AND`!
hint: To combine two conditions that both must be true, use the `AND` keyword.

title: Flexible Conditions: Sales or Marketing
instruction: We need to contact everyone in either the 'Sales' department OR the 'Marketing' department. Show all details for employees who belong to either of these departments from the `employees` table. (Assume a 'Marketing' department exists in your dataset for this exercise, even if empty).
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = 'Sales' OR department = 'Marketing'
successMsg: Great! You can now use `OR` to find data that meets at least one of several conditions.
hint: Use `OR` when you want rows that satisfy *any* of the given conditions.

title: Alphabetical Order: Employee Names
instruction: Our HR team needs an alphabetical list of all employees by their `name`. Retrieve all employee details from the `employees` table, sorted by `name` in ascending order.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM employees ORDER BY name ASC
successMsg: Nicely done! Sorting data makes it much easier to read.
hint: The `ORDER BY` clause is used for sorting. `ASC` is for ascending, `DESC` for descending. `ASC` is often the default.

title: Top Earners: Highest Salary First
instruction: Who are our highest-paid employees? Show all employee details, but this time, order them by `salary` in descending order, so the highest salaries appear first.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC
successMsg: Fantastic! You can now identify your top performers based on salary.
hint: To sort from highest to lowest, use `DESC` after the column name in `ORDER BY`.

title: Organized by Department, Then Name
instruction: For a new organizational chart, we need employees sorted first by `department` (alphabetically), and then within each department, by `name` (alphabetically). Show all details from the `employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM employees ORDER BY department ASC, name ASC
successMsg: Excellent! You've mastered multi-column sorting for even better data organization.
hint: You can specify multiple columns in the `ORDER BY` clause, separated by commas. SQL will sort by the first, then the second, and so on.

title: Just the Top 3 Employees
instruction: We only need to see the first 3 employees listed by their `id`. Retrieve all details for the top 3 employees from the `employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM employees ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT 3
successMsg: Great! `LIMIT` is essential for handling large datasets and showing only a subset.
hint: Use `LIMIT N` to retrieve only the first `N` rows after any `ORDER BY` clause.

title: How Many Employees Do We Have?
instruction: Quickly, how many employees are there in total? Use an aggregate function to count all rows in the `employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_employees FROM employees
successMsg: You've successfully counted all employees! `COUNT(*)` is a fundamental aggregate function.
hint: The `COUNT(*)` function counts the total number of rows. You can often give the result a temporary name using `AS`.

title: Total Monthly Payroll
instruction: What's the combined total of all employee salaries for our monthly payroll? Calculate the sum of all `salary` values from the `employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT SUM(salary) AS total_payroll FROM employees
successMsg: Excellent! You can now calculate sums for numeric columns.
hint: Use the `SUM()` function to add up values in a numeric column.

title: Average Employee Salary
instruction: What's the average salary across all our employees? Calculate the average of the `salary` column from the `employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT AVG(salary) AS average_salary FROM employees
successMsg: Well done! You can now find the average of numerical data.
hint: The `AVG()` function calculates the arithmetic mean of a numeric column.

title: Salary Range: Lowest and Highest
instruction: HR wants to know the minimum and maximum salary paid to any employee. Find both the `MIN` and `MAX` `salary` from the `employees` table in a single query.
expectedQuery: SELECT MIN(salary) AS min_salary, MAX(salary) AS max_salary FROM employees
successMsg: Fantastic! Identifying value ranges is crucial for data analysis.
hint: You can select multiple aggregate functions in one `SELECT` statement, separating them with commas.

title: Employees Per Department
instruction: How many employees are in each department? Count the number of employees for each unique `department` in the `employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS num_employees FROM employees GROUP BY department ORDER BY department
successMsg: Excellent use of `GROUP BY`! You can now categorize and count data.
hint: When using aggregate functions to count items in groups, you need to specify the grouping column(s) with `GROUP BY`.

title: Average Salary Per Department
instruction: Management wants to know the average `salary` for each `department`. Calculate this from the `employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_dept_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department ORDER BY department
successMsg: Great job! Grouped averages provide valuable insights into departmental spending.
hint: Combine `AVG()` with `GROUP BY` to get averages for distinct categories.

title: Departments with High Average Salary
instruction: Which departments have an average `salary` greater than $70,000? Show the `department` and its `avg_dept_salary` from the `employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_dept_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING AVG(salary) > 70000 ORDER BY department
successMsg: You've successfully filtered groups using `HAVING`! Very powerful.
hint: `HAVING` is like `WHERE` but for filtering *grouped* results after aggregation. It comes after `GROUP BY`.

title: Unique Departments
instruction: Just list all the unique `department` names we have. No duplicates, please! Use the `DISTINCT` keyword on the `employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT DISTINCT department FROM employees ORDER BY department
successMsg: Excellent! `DISTINCT` helps you quickly see all unique values in a column.
hint: Place `DISTINCT` right after `SELECT` and before the column name to get unique values.

title: Employees and Their Project Assignments
instruction: We have two tables: `employees` (id, name, department, salary) and `projects` (project_id, project_name, employee_id). Find the `name` of each employee and the `project_name` of the project they are assigned to. Link these two tables using their common `id` from `employees` and `employee_id` from `projects`.
expectedQuery: SELECT e.name, p.project_name FROM employees e JOIN projects p ON e.id = p.employee_id ORDER BY e.name
successMsg: You've completed your first `JOIN`! Connecting data from multiple tables is a core SQL skill. Well done!
hint: Use `JOIN` to combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them. Specify the join condition with `ON`.

title: Welcome to the Academy: See All Students!
instruction: Welcome, new recruit! Your first mission is to retrieve ALL information about our 'Students'. We need to see every column and every row from the `Students` table. Your query should use `SELECT *`.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Students
successMsg: Excellent! You've successfully viewed all student data. That's a great start!
hint: To select all columns from a table, use `SELECT *` followed by `FROM` and the table name.

title: Product Showcase: Name and Price
instruction: Our marketing team needs a quick list of product names and their prices from the `Products` table. Don't worry about other details like category or ID, just the name and price for each product.
expectedQuery: SELECT name, price FROM Products
successMsg: Fantastic! The marketing team has exactly what they need. You're getting the hang of selecting specific columns.
hint: List the column names you want to see, separated by commas, after `SELECT`.

title: Employee Roster: First Name and Department
instruction: The HR department is reorganizing and needs a list of all employees showing their first name and the department they belong to. Fetch this information from the `Employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT first_name, department FROM Employees
successMsg: Perfect! HR can now easily see who works where. Good job focusing on the requested columns!
hint: Remember to specify exactly which columns you need after `SELECT`.

title: Customer Order History: Customer 101
instruction: A specific customer, with `customer_id` 101, is asking about their past orders. Retrieve all details for every order placed by this customer from the `Orders` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE customer_id = 101
successMsg: Excellent filtering! Customer 101's order history is now clear.
hint: Use the `WHERE` clause to filter rows based on a condition, like `column_name = value`.

title: Library Catalog: Fantasy Books
instruction: Our library wants to showcase all books from the 'Fantasy' genre. Please retrieve all details for every book in the `Books` table where the `genre` is 'Fantasy'.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Books WHERE genre = 'Fantasy'
successMsg: Great! The Fantasy section is now perfectly organized.
hint: When filtering by text (strings), remember to enclose the text in single quotes, e.g., `'Text'`.

title: Modern Cinema: Movies Released After 2000
instruction: The cinema club is only interested in modern films. Show them all details of movies from the `Movies` table that were released `after the year 2000`. This means the `release_year` should be greater than 2000.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Movies WHERE release_year > 2000
successMsg: Fantastic! Only the latest and greatest films for the cinema club.
hint: You can use comparison operators like `>` (greater than), `<` (less than), `>=` (greater than or equal to), and `<=` (less than or equal to) in your `WHERE` clause.

title: Course Selection: Computer Science with 3 Credits
instruction: Students are looking for specific courses: those offered by the 'Computer Science' department AND worth exactly 3 credits. Find all details for such courses from the `Courses` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Courses WHERE department = 'Computer Science' AND credits = 3
successMsg: Spot on! These are the exact courses students were looking for. Combining conditions works!
hint: Use the `AND` operator to combine multiple conditions, requiring all of them to be true.

title: Showroom Inventory: Toyota or Honda Vehicles
instruction: Our showroom needs to display all vehicles from either 'Toyota' OR 'Honda'. Retrieve all information for these vehicles from the `Vehicles` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Vehicles WHERE make = 'Toyota' OR make = 'Honda'
successMsg: Excellent! The showroom now has a perfectly filtered list of vehicles. You're a master of logical operators!
hint: Use the `OR` operator when at least one of the conditions must be true.

title: Game Leaderboard: Lowest Scores First
instruction: We're setting up a 'lowest score wins' leaderboard for our new game. Display all game scores from the `Scores` table, ordered from the lowest score to the highest. (Ascending order is the default if you just use ORDER BY, but it's good practice to specify ASC!)
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Scores ORDER BY score ASC
successMsg: You've successfully sorted the scores! The lowest score winner is clear.
hint: Use `ORDER BY column_name ASC` to sort results in ascending order.

title: Transaction Review: Highest Amounts First
instruction: Our finance department needs to review the largest transactions first. List all transactions from the `Transactions` table, ordered by `amount` from highest to lowest.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Transactions ORDER BY amount DESC
successMsg: Excellent! The finance team can now prioritize their review. Ordering by amount DESC worked perfectly!
hint: Use `ORDER BY column_name DESC` to sort results in descending order.

title: New User Outreach: Early Birds by Username
instruction: We want to send a special welcome to users who registered before 2023-01-01. Retrieve all their details from the `Users` table and display them sorted alphabetically by their `username`.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Users WHERE registration_date < '2023-01-01' ORDER BY username ASC
successMsg: Fantastic! The early bird users are now identified and sorted. You're mastering multi-clause queries!
hint: Combine `WHERE` and `ORDER BY` clauses. `WHERE` comes before `ORDER BY`.

title: Top Stories: First Two Articles
instruction: Our homepage can only display the first two articles. Fetch the complete details for the first 2 articles from the `Articles` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Articles LIMIT 2
successMsg: Excellent! Only the top two articles are displayed. `LIMIT` is a powerful tool!
hint: Use `LIMIT N` at the end of your query to restrict the number of rows returned.

title: Game Champions: Top 2 High Scores
instruction: The 'Game Champions' section needs to show the top 2 highest scores. Retrieve the player's name, score, and game date from the `HighScores` table, ordered by `score` in descending order, and limited to only the top 2 entries.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM HighScores ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 2
successMsg: Champion effort! You've successfully identified the top 2 players.
hint: `ORDER BY` usually comes before `LIMIT` when you want to get the 'top N' records.

title: Workforce Size: Count All Employees
instruction: Our CEO wants to know the total number of employees in the company. Count all entries in the `Employees` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Employees
successMsg: Precisely! The CEO now knows the exact number of employees. Aggregations are key!
hint: Use the `COUNT(*)` function to count all rows in a table. It's an aggregation function, so it will return a single row with the count.

title: Inventory Check: How Many Electronics?
instruction: The inventory manager needs to know how many products fall under the 'Electronics' category. Count only the products from the `Products` table where the `category` is 'Electronics'.
expectedQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Products WHERE category = 'Electronics'
successMsg: Inventory updated! You successfully counted specific items.
hint: You can combine `COUNT(*)` with a `WHERE` clause to count rows that meet a certain condition.

title: Sales Performance: Average Sale Amount
instruction: The sales team wants to understand their average sale performance. Calculate the average `amount` of all sales recorded in the `Sales` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT AVG(amount) FROM Sales
successMsg: Spot on! The sales team now has a clear picture of their average sale. AVG is a useful aggregate!
hint: The `AVG()` function calculates the average value of a numeric column. You can round your result if you wish, but for this level, the direct average is fine.

title: Customer Activity: Orders Per Customer
instruction: We need to understand our customer's ordering habits. For each `customer_id`, count how many orders they have placed from the `Orders` table. Label the count column `total_orders`.
expectedQuery: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS total_orders FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_id
successMsg: Fantastic! You've successfully grouped and counted orders per customer. GROUP BY is powerful!
hint: Use `GROUP BY` with the `customer_id` column to group orders, then `COUNT(*)` to count orders within each group. Use `AS` to rename the `COUNT(*)` column.

title: Account Balances: Total Transactions Per Account
instruction: Our bank needs to know the total `amount` of all transactions for each `account_id` from the `Transactions` table. Calculate the sum of amounts for each account and label it `total_amount`.
expectedQuery: SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) AS total_amount FROM Transactions GROUP BY account_id
successMsg: Excellent! Account balances summarized. SUM and GROUP BY are essential for financial analysis!
hint: Similar to `COUNT`, use the `SUM()` function with `GROUP BY` to aggregate amounts for each `account_id`.

title: Customer Orders: Linking Customers and Orders
instruction: We want to see the `name` of each customer and the `total_amount` of their orders. You'll need to combine information from the `Customers` and `Orders` tables using a `JOIN`. Remember to use aliases for tables to make your query shorter!
expectedQuery: SELECT C.name, O.total_amount FROM Customers AS C JOIN Orders AS O ON C.customer_id = O.customer_id
successMsg: Wonderful! You've successfully linked customer and order data. Joins are fundamental to relational databases!
hint: Use `JOIN table2 ON table1.common_column = table2.common_column`. Aliases like `C` for `Customers` and `O` for `Orders` are helpful.

title: Department Review: New York Employees
instruction: The HR department needs a list of employee `name`s and their `department_name` for all departments located in 'New York'. You'll need to `JOIN` `Employees` and `Departments` tables, then filter the results.
expectedQuery: SELECT E.name, D.department_name FROM Employees AS E JOIN Departments AS D ON E.department_id = D.department_id WHERE D.location = 'New York'
successMsg: Congratulations, SQL Master! You've successfully performed a multi-table query with filtering. You're ready for more advanced SQL!
hint: Combine `JOIN` and `WHERE` clauses. The `WHERE` clause comes after the `JOIN` clause.

title: Welcome to SQL Academy!
instruction: Welcome, new recruit! Your first mission: retrieve ALL data from the `Students` table. Use the wildcard character.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Students
successMsg: Excellent work! You've successfully selected all columns. The '*' is a powerful shorthand!
hint: Remember the universal selector: '*'. And don't forget 'FROM' to specify the table.

title: Picking Specific Columns
instruction: We don't always need everything. This time, I only want to see the `name` and `major` of all students. List the column names explicitly.
expectedQuery: SELECT name, major FROM Students
successMsg: Perfect! You've learned to select specific data points. This saves bandwidth and focuses your query.
hint: Instead of '*', list the column names separated by commas after SELECT.

title: Filtering with WHERE: Equality
instruction: Our dean wants to find all students who are majoring in 'Computer Science'. Use the `WHERE` clause to filter the results.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Students WHERE major = 'Computer Science'
successMsg: Fantastic! You've mastered basic filtering. The WHERE clause is essential for precise data retrieval.
hint: Add 'WHERE' followed by the column, an equals sign, and the value (remember quotes for text!).

title: Filtering with WHERE: Numeric Comparison
instruction: Now, let's find all students older than 20. Use the `age` column and a comparison operator.
expectedQuery: SELECT name, age FROM Students WHERE age > 20
successMsg: Excellent! You can now filter based on numerical conditions. Keep an eye on those operators!
hint: Use '>' for 'greater than'. Numeric values don't need quotes.

title: Filtering with WHERE: LIKE for Partial Matches
instruction: A student's name might be misspelled or we only remember part of it. Find all students whose name starts with 'B'. Use the `LIKE` operator with a wildcard.
expectedQuery: SELECT name FROM Students WHERE name LIKE 'B%'
successMsg: Great job with `LIKE`! The '%' wildcard is incredibly useful for pattern matching.
hint: Use 'LIKE' and the '%' wildcard. For names starting with 'B', it would be 'B%'.

title: Combining Conditions: AND Operator
instruction: We need to find students who are 'Computer Science' majors AND are older than 20. Combine two conditions using `AND`.
expectedQuery: SELECT name, major, age FROM Students WHERE major = 'Computer Science' AND age > 20
successMsg: You've successfully used `AND`! This allows for very precise filtering, requiring both conditions to be true.
hint: Place `AND` between your two `WHERE` conditions. Remember the previous challenges for each part.

title: Combining Conditions: OR Operator
instruction: Now, let's find students who are either 'Physics' majors OR 'Mathematics' majors. Use the `OR` operator.
expectedQuery: SELECT name, major FROM Students WHERE major = 'Physics' OR major = 'Mathematics'
successMsg: Excellent use of `OR`! Now you can retrieve data where at least one of your conditions is met.
hint: Place `OR` between the two conditions for the `major` column.

title: Filtering with NOT Operator
instruction: Show me all students who are NOT 'Computer Science' majors. Use the `NOT` operator.
expectedQuery: SELECT name, major FROM Students WHERE NOT major = 'Computer Science'
successMsg: Nicely done! The `NOT` operator is great for excluding specific data points from your results.
hint: Put `NOT` before your condition in the `WHERE` clause.

title: Filtering with IN Operator
instruction: Instead of multiple ORs, let's find students majoring in 'Physics' or 'Mathematics' using the `IN` operator. It's cleaner!
expectedQuery: SELECT name, major FROM Students WHERE major IN ('Physics', 'Mathematics')
successMsg: Fantastic! `IN` is a powerful way to check for multiple possible values efficiently.
hint: Use `IN` followed by a list of values in parentheses, separated by commas.

title: Filtering with BETWEEN Operator
instruction: Find all students whose `age` is between 20 and 22 (inclusive). Use the `BETWEEN` operator.
expectedQuery: SELECT name, age FROM Students WHERE age BETWEEN 20 AND 22
successMsg: Excellent use of `BETWEEN`! It makes range queries much simpler and more readable.
hint: The syntax is `column BETWEEN value1 AND value2`.

title: Ordering Results: ASCENDING
instruction: Let's get organized! Retrieve all student names and ages, ordered by `age` from youngest to oldest.
expectedQuery: SELECT name, age FROM Students ORDER BY age ASC
successMsg: Brilliant! `ORDER BY` with `ASC` is crucial for arranging your data in a logical sequence.
hint: Add `ORDER BY` followed by the column name and `ASC` for ascending order (or omit `ASC` as it's the default).

title: Ordering Results: DESCENDING
instruction: Now, order the students by `age` from oldest to youngest. This time, specify `DESC`.
expectedQuery: SELECT name, age FROM Students ORDER BY age DESC
successMsg: Perfect! `DESC` allows you to reverse the order, which is great for finding the latest or highest values.
hint: Use `DESC` after the column name in your `ORDER BY` clause.

title: Limiting Results: The TOP N
instruction: We only need the `name` of the top 2 oldest students. Combine `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`.
expectedQuery: SELECT name FROM Students ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 2
successMsg: Excellent! `LIMIT` is incredibly useful for fetching only a subset of data, especially for performance or 'top N' reports.
hint: First, `ORDER BY age DESC`, then add `LIMIT 2` at the very end of your query.

title: Counting Records: COUNT()
instruction: How many students do we have in total? Use the `COUNT(*)` aggregate function.
expectedQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Students
successMsg: You've successfully counted all records! `COUNT(*)` is a fundamental function for getting record totals.
hint: Simply `SELECT COUNT(*)` and specify the `FROM` table.

title: Counting with a Condition: COUNT() + WHERE
instruction: How many students are majoring in 'Computer Science'? Combine `COUNT(*)` with a `WHERE` clause.
expectedQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Students WHERE major = 'Computer Science'
successMsg: Great job! You can now get counts for specific subsets of your data. Very useful!
hint: Your `WHERE` clause goes after the `FROM` clause, just like before.

title: Summing Values: SUM()
instruction: We've added a `score` column. What's the total `score` of all students? Use the `SUM()` aggregate function.
expectedQuery: SELECT SUM(score) FROM Students
successMsg: Awesome! `SUM()` is perfect for calculating totals from numerical columns.
hint: The new `Students` table data will be: `student_id`, `name`, `age`, `major`, `score`. Use `SELECT SUM(score)`.

title: Averaging Values: AVG()
instruction: What's the average `score` of all students? Use the `AVG()` aggregate function.
expectedQuery: SELECT AVG(score) FROM Students
successMsg: Excellent! `AVG()` provides a quick way to find the mean of a numerical set.
hint: Use `SELECT AVG(score)`.

title: Min & Max Values: MIN() and MAX()
instruction: Find the highest (`MAX`) and lowest (`MIN`) `score` among all students. Select both in a single query.
expectedQuery: SELECT MAX(score), MIN(score) FROM Students
successMsg: Well done! `MIN()` and `MAX()` are essential for quickly finding extreme values in your data.
hint: You can select multiple aggregate functions, separated by commas, in a single `SELECT` statement.

title: Grouping Aggregations: GROUP BY
instruction: How many students are there in each `major`? Use `GROUP BY` with `COUNT(*)` to get counts per major.
expectedQuery: SELECT major, COUNT(*) FROM Students GROUP BY major
successMsg: Fantastic! `GROUP BY` is a cornerstone of analytical SQL, letting you summarize data by categories.
hint: First, select the `major` column and `COUNT(*)`. Then, add `GROUP BY major`.

title: Connecting Tables: INNER JOIN
instruction: We have `Students` and `Courses` tables. Each student enrolls in a course. Show the `name` of each student and the `course_title` they are enrolled in. Join the tables on `course_id`.
expectedQuery: SELECT S.name, C.course_title FROM Students S INNER JOIN Courses C ON S.course_id = C.course_id
successMsg: Congratulations, you've completed the academy's beginner levels! Joining tables is a critical skill for real-world databases.
hint: Start with `SELECT S.name, C.course_title FROM Students S`. Then use `INNER JOIN Courses C ON S.course_id = C.course_id`. The Students table now includes a `course_id` column. The Courses table has `course_id` and `course_title`.

title: Welcome to the Academy!
instruction: You've just enrolled in the SQL Academy! Let's start by getting familiar with our student roster. Your first task is to view all information about all students. Select all columns and all rows from the `Students` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Students
successMsg: Excellent! You've successfully viewed the entire student table. On to the next challenge!
hint: Use the '*' wildcard to select all columns.

title: Focusing on Key Information
instruction: The administration often needs to see just a subset of information for privacy reasons. Now, they only want to see the `name` and `age` of each student. Select only these two columns from the `Students` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT name, age FROM Students
successMsg: Perfect! You've learned how to pick specific columns. Keep up the great work!
hint: List the column names you want, separated by commas, after SELECT.

title: Filtering by Age
instruction: Our academic advisor wants to identify all students who are exactly 18 years old for a special orientation. Retrieve all columns for students whose `age` is 18 from the `Students` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT student_id, name, age, major FROM Students WHERE age = 18
successMsg: Fantastic! You've used the WHERE clause to filter numerical data effectively.
hint: Add a WHERE clause followed by your condition (e.g., column_name = value).

title: Department Specific Courses
instruction: The 'IT' department is planning their course schedule and needs a list of all courses they offer. Select all columns from the `Courses` table where the `department` is 'IT'.
expectedQuery: SELECT course_id, title, department FROM Courses WHERE department = 'IT'
successMsg: Excellent! You've successfully filtered by a string value. Remember quotes for strings!
hint: String values in the WHERE clause need to be enclosed in single quotes.

title: High Achievers
instruction: We want to recognize students who are performing exceptionally well. Find all enrollments from the `Grades` table where the `score` is greater than 90. Show all columns for these enrollments.
expectedQuery: SELECT enrollment_id, student_id, score FROM Grades WHERE score > 90
successMsg: Great job! Identifying high scores is crucial. You're mastering numerical comparisons.
hint: Use comparison operators like > (greater than), < (less than), >= (greater than or equal to), etc.

title: Combining Conditions (AND)
instruction: The Dean wants a very specific list: students who are 18 years old AND are majoring in 'Computer Science'. Select the `student_id`, `name`, `age`, and `major` for these students from the `Students` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT student_id, name, age, major FROM Students WHERE age = 18 AND major = 'Computer Science'
successMsg: Superb! Combining conditions with AND helps you pinpoint very specific data.
hint: Use the AND keyword to link two conditions. Both must be true for a row to be returned.

title: Flexible Filtering (OR)
instruction: Students are looking for elective courses. They are interested in either 'Art' or 'Music' courses. Find all courses from the `Courses` table that belong to either the 'Art' OR 'Music' department. Show all columns.
expectedQuery: SELECT course_id, title, department FROM Courses WHERE department = 'Art' OR department = 'Music'
successMsg: Excellent! You've mastered filtering with OR. Now they have their electives!
hint: Use the OR keyword to link two conditions. If either is true, the row is returned.

title: Alphabetical Order
instruction: The registrar needs a list of all students, sorted alphabetically by their `name` in ascending order. Select `student_id`, `name`, and `age` from the `Students` table and order the results.
expectedQuery: SELECT student_id, name, age FROM Students ORDER BY name ASC
successMsg: Well sorted! Ordering data makes it much easier to read and analyze.
hint: Use ORDER BY followed by the column name and ASC for ascending order (or it's the default).

title: Top Scorers First
instruction: We want to celebrate our top academic performers! Show `student_id` and `score` from the `Grades` table, sorted by `score` in descending order to see the highest scores at the top.
expectedQuery: SELECT student_id, score FROM Grades ORDER BY score DESC
successMsg: Fantastic! You've correctly ordered by score, showing our highest achievers.
hint: Use ORDER BY followed by the column name and DESC for descending order.

title: Multi-level Sorting
instruction: The faculty wants to review students, first by their `major` (alphabetically) and then by their `age` (oldest first) within each major. Select `name`, `age`, and `major` from `Students`.
expectedQuery: SELECT name, age, major FROM Students ORDER BY major ASC, age DESC
successMsg: Impressive! Sorting by multiple columns gives you precise control over data presentation.
hint: List multiple columns after ORDER BY, separated by commas, each with its own ASC/DESC.

title: Limiting Results
instruction: The course catalog is quite extensive. For a quick preview, the academic committee only wants to see the first 3 course `title`s and `course_id`s from the `Courses` table. Ignore any specific order for now.
expectedQuery: SELECT course_id, title FROM Courses LIMIT 3
successMsg: Well done! Limiting results is a practical way to manage large datasets.
hint: Add LIMIT followed by the number of rows you want at the end of your query.

title: Counting All Students
instruction: The administration needs an exact count of all students enrolled in the Academy. Count all rows in the `Students` table and label the resulting column `total_students`.
expectedQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_students FROM Students
successMsg: Excellent counting! Aggregate functions like COUNT are essential for summaries.
hint: Use COUNT(*) for a total count of rows, and AS to rename the output column.

title: Counting Unique Departments
instruction: How diverse is our course offering? We want to know how many *unique* departments offer courses. Count the distinct `department` values from the `Courses` table and label it `total_departments`.
expectedQuery: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT department) AS total_departments FROM Courses
successMsg: Great! You've found the number of unique departments. DISTINCT is a powerful tool!
hint: Use COUNT(DISTINCT column_name) to count only unique values in a column.

title: Total Tuition Collected
instruction: The finance department needs to know the total amount of `tuition_paid` across all students for auditing purposes. Sum the `amount` column from the `Payments` table and label it `total_tuition_paid`.
expectedQuery: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total_tuition_paid FROM Payments
successMsg: Money matters! You've successfully summed up all tuition payments.
hint: The SUM() function calculates the total of a numeric column. Don't forget AS to rename!

title: Average Performance
instruction: What's the overall academic performance of our students? Calculate the average `score` across all enrollments from the `Grades` table and label it `average_score`.
expectedQuery: SELECT AVG(score) AS average_score FROM Grades
successMsg: Spot on! Calculating averages gives a great overview of performance.
hint: Use the AVG() function for average values. Remember to use AS.

title: Extremes in Grading
instruction: The testing department wants to know the `highest_score` and `lowest_score` ever recorded in any enrollment. Select both as `highest_score` and `lowest_score` from the `Grades` table.
expectedQuery: SELECT MAX(score) AS highest_score, MIN(score) AS lowest_score FROM Grades
successMsg: Excellent! You've found the boundaries of our grading system.
hint: MAX() finds the highest value, and MIN() finds the lowest value in a column. Use AS for both.

title: Students Per Major
instruction: The Dean needs to see how many students are enrolled in each `major`. Group the students by their `major` and count the `num_students` in each group. Select the `major` and `num_students`.
expectedQuery: SELECT major, COUNT(student_id) AS num_students FROM Students GROUP BY major
successMsg: Perfect! Grouping data reveals insightful statistics for each category.
hint: Use GROUP BY with the column you want to group by. Any non-aggregated columns in SELECT must be in GROUP BY.

title: Individual Student Payments
instruction: The finance department now wants a breakdown: the `total_paid` amount for each `student_id`. Group the `Payments` table by `student_id` and sum their `amount`.
expectedQuery: SELECT student_id, SUM(amount) AS total_paid FROM Payments GROUP BY student_id
successMsg: Outstanding! You can now see each student's total contribution.
hint: Combine SUM() with GROUP BY to aggregate values for distinct groups.

title: Linking Students to Enrollments
instruction: It's time to connect the dots! We need to link students to their course enrollments. Join the `Students` table with the `Enrollments` table on `student_id`. Select `Students.name` (aliased as `student_name`), `Enrollments.enrollment_id`, and `Enrollments.course_id`.
expectedQuery: SELECT S.name AS student_name, E.enrollment_id, E.course_id FROM Students S JOIN Enrollments E ON S.student_id = E.student_id
successMsg: Congratulations! You've successfully performed your first JOIN. Data relationships are now clear!
hint: Use the JOIN keyword, specify the second table, and then ON to define the matching columns. Use table aliases (e.g., S for Students) to shorten your query.

title: Top Performing Students (Joined & Filtered)
instruction: For your final challenge, identify the names of students who scored above 90. Join the `Students` and `Grades` tables on `student_id`. Select `Students.name` (aliased as `student_name`) and `Grades.score`, but only for students with a `score` greater than 90.
expectedQuery: SELECT S.name AS student_name, G.score FROM Students S JOIN Grades G ON S.student_id = G.student_id WHERE G.score > 90
successMsg: You've done it! You've combined joining, filtering, and selecting specific data. You are now a SQL Academy graduate!

title: Finding Patterns with LIKE

title: Sorting Results (ASC)

expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Students ORDER BY Grade ASC

title: Sorting Results (DESC)

expectedQuery: SELECT * FROM Scores ORDER BY Score DESC

title: Limiting Your Results

title: Counting Rows with COUNT()

title: Summing Values with SUM()

title: Grouping Data (COUNT)

title: Joining Two Tables
instruction: You have 'Orders' and 'Customers' tables. Combine them to see which customer ('CustomerName') placed each 'OrderID'. You'll need to join them using the common 'CustomerID'.

title: Joining and Selecting Specifics
instruction: Now, let's get a bit more precise with joins. Display only the 'ProductName' from the 'Products' table and its corresponding 'CategoryName' from the 'Categories' table.
expectedQuery: SELECT Products.ProductName, Categories.CategoryName FROM Products INNER JOIN Categories ON Products.CategoryID = Categories.CategoryID
successMsg: Excellent! You're selecting just the right information from joined tables.

title: Filtering Joined Data
instruction: The HR department wants to see which employees work in the 'Sales' department. Join the 'Employees' and 'Departments' tables, then filter the results to only show employees in the 'Sales' department.

title: Joining and Ordering Data
instruction: For a comprehensive report, list all orders, their customer names, and cities. Then, order the entire result set by the customer's 'CustomerName' alphabetically.
